alalal-e93748-d1e104.summary: Rubric of Article 8: whether the centurion Cornelius had faith in the incarnation before Peter came to him.

alalal-e93748-d1e115.summary: Introduces the question on Lombard's chapter 'Solet etiam quaeri de Cornelio'.

alalal-e93748-d1e124.summary: Notes the question arises chiefly from Augustine's words cited in the text.

alalal-e93748-d1e132.summary: First objection: faith is first, so Cornelius did not come to faith through mercy but rather to mercy through faith.

alalal-e93748-d1e143.summary: Second objection: one would not pray to one in whom one in no way believed, as Augustine says, so it seems false that Peter was sent to teach him faith; and if Cornelius had implicit faith that Peter made explicit, this fails because Cornelius was one of the 'greater' who should have had explicit faith.

alalal-e93748-d1e167.summary: Solution: Cornelius had explicit faith, though implicit would have sufficed, since he was 'greater' only in rank, not in revelation. His explicit faith concerned Christ's incarnation as related to any time; so Peter, architect of the Church, was sent to determine the article he believed explicitly to a definite time, so that he would no longer await as future one whom Peter taught had come. Augustine's 'instruct in the faith' means determining the faith, not explaining the article, and this determination belongs to faith as it comes from hearing.
claims: Cornelius explicitly believed in the incarnation without knowing that it had already occurred.
Peter was sent to fix the time of the incarnation for him, not to give him new faith.

alalal-e93748.summary: Article 8 asks whether Cornelius had faith in the incarnation before Peter came, given Augustine's view that he prayed to God and that Peter was sent to teach him the faith. Albert holds that Cornelius had explicit faith in the incarnation, though implicit faith would have sufficed, since he was 'greater' only in rank, not in revelation. His faith was indeterminate as to time. Peter was sent to determine the article to a definite time, teaching that the one awaited had already come. This determination belongs to faith from hearing and adds no new article.
claims: Cornelius explicitly believed in the incarnation without knowing when it occurred.
Peter's instruction determined the time of the article rather than giving new faith.
